name: Injection moulding
source: ecoinvent average, in Elduque et al., Materials 11:1740 (2018)
note: Electricity only; range 1,000–2,100 kWh per t of plastic injected

name: Film and sheet extrusion
source: R. Kent, Plastics Technology (2009), typical extrusion plant process load
note: Electricity only; range 400–600 kWh/t; film slightly below profile

name: Pipe and profile extrusion
source: R. Kent, Plastics Technology (2009), typical extrusion plant process load
note: Electricity only; range 400–600 kWh/t (example profile plant 449)

name: Extrusion blow moulding (bottles, containers)
source: R. Kent, Plastics Technology (2009), typical blow moulding site
note: Electricity only; range 1,400–2,500 kWh/t

name: Sheet extrusion and thermoforming (trays, cups)
source: R. Kent, Plastics Technology (2009), inline sheet extrusion + thermoforming
note: Electricity only; range 900–1,600 kWh/t; includes making the sheet

name: Mechanical recycling to pellets (shred, wash, extrude)
source: Sevigné-Itoiz et al., Waste Management 46 (2015), Europe
note: Electricity; Europe 270–330 kWh/t, China 575

name: Hot rolling (strip, plate, bars)
source: US DOE Iron & Steel Bandwidth Study (2015): typical 3.00 GJ/t; split 19 % electricity as LBNL world best practice (2007)
note: Total 833 kWh/t; the electricity/heat split is taken from LBNL-62806 strip rolling (83 kWh electricity, 365 kWh fuel per t)

name: Cold rolling and annealing
source: LBNL-62806 world best practice (2007) + EU BAT conclusions FMP 2022/2110 (annealing)
note: Electricity 87 kWh/t and 53 kWh/t steam and fuel (LBNL); annealing 167–333 kWh/t fuel (BAT, midpoint 250). Best practice: typical plants use more (US DOE typical total 1,125 kWh/t)

name: Batch hot-dip galvanising
source: EU BAT conclusions, Ferrous Metals Processing (2022/2110)
note: 300–800 kWh/t (midpoint), mostly fuel for the zinc kettle and drying; counted as natural gas

name: Extrusion (incl. billet heating)
source: US DOE Aluminum Bandwidth Study (2016), typical on-site 2,948 Btu/lb
note: Total 1,905 kWh/t; electricity share derived from DOE off-site losses

name: Hot rolling
source: US DOE Aluminum Bandwidth Study (2016), typical on-site 1,814 Btu/lb
note: Total 1,172 kWh/t; electricity share derived from DOE off-site losses

name: Cold rolling (sheet, foil)
source: US DOE Aluminum Bandwidth Study (2016), typical on-site 1,511 Btu/lb
note: Total 976 kWh/t; electricity share derived from DOE off-site losses

name: Remelting and casting (from ingot or scrap)
source: US DOE Aluminum Bandwidth Study (2016), typical on-site 2,229 Btu/lb
note: Total 1,440 kWh/t; electricity share derived from DOE off-site losses

name: Corrugated board and box making (from containerboard)
source: FEFCO / Cepi ContainerBoard, European Database for Corrugated Board Life Cycle Studies (2023 edition, 2022 data)
note: Bought electricity 0.441 GJ/t; natural gas 0.836 and steam 0.066 GJ/t of net saleable product

name: Wheat flour milling
source: EU BAT conclusions, Food, Drink and Milk (2019/2031)
note: 50–130 kWh per t of products, total energy (midpoint); milling is almost all electricity, so counted as electricity

name: Edible oil refining
source: EU BAT conclusions, Food, Drink and Milk (2019/2031), stand-alone refining
note: 100–450 kWh per t of oil, total energy (midpoint); mostly steam, counted as natural gas

name: Dairy: market milk (pasteurised, packed)
source: UNEP / Danish EPA, Cleaner Production Assessment in Dairy Processing (2000)
note: Electricity 0.20 GJ/t and fuel 0.46 GJ/t of product (older survey); EU BAT total 100–600 kWh/t raw milk

name: Dairy: cheese making
source: UNEP / Danish EPA, Cleaner Production Assessment in Dairy Processing (2000)
note: Electricity 0.76 GJ/t and fuel 4.34 GJ/t of cheese (older survey)

name: Bread baking (oven)
source: EU JRC, Best Environmental Management Practice – food and beverage, baking (citing Purlis 2012)
note: 3.7–7 MJ/kg for the oven only (midpoint); counted as natural gas — electric ovens: enter the energy instead

name: Yarn spinning
source: Hasanbeigi et al., LBNL-5753E (2012)
note: Median of 3 mills: electricity 3,600–6,600 kWh/t, fuel 1,972–3,444 kWh/t of yarn; small sample

name: Weaving
source: Hasanbeigi et al., LBNL-5753E (2012)
note: Mean of 2 plants: electricity 1,200–2,200 kWh/t, fuel 2,972–4,806 kWh/t of fabric; small sample

name: Dyeing and finishing (wet processing)
source: Hasanbeigi et al., LBNL-5753E (2012)
note: Median of 3 plants: electricity 1,500–2,500, fuel/steam 11,194–31,167 kWh/t of finished fabric; small sample

name: Container glass melting and forming (from cullet and batch)
source: US DOE Glass Bandwidth Study (2017), container glass typical 6.91 MMBtu/ton
note: Total 2,013 kWh/t of finished glass; split 96 % fuel / 4 % electricity as assumed by DOE; each 10 % cullet saves 2.5–3 %

name: Cement grinding (clinker and additives to cement)
source: WBCSD-CSI / ECRA Technology Papers (2017)
note: 43 % of the global average 104 kWh electricity per t of cement; best practice 25–31 kWh/t

name: Hot mix asphalt production
source: NAPA / Mukherjee, Update to the LCA for Asphalt Mixtures (2021)
note: Per t of mix, converted from US short tons; dryer burner counted as natural gas

name: Tyre manufacturing (mixing, building, curing)
source: PBL / TNO, Decarbonisation options for the Dutch tyre industry (2019)
note: One plant, per t of tyre, including mixing; US DOE whole-site figure is higher (5,212 kWh/t)
